source.title: RynnVLA-Latent: Scaling Robotic Manipulation Foundation Models with 3D-Grounded Latent Actions
source.authors: Hao-Yu Zhao; Xing-Yue Zhao; Zhian Su; Bo-Han Hou; Yin-Zhou Tang; Feng-Yi Wang; Ke-Han Li; Yu-Ming Jiang; Zhen-Yu Zeng; Ming-Xiu Chen; De-Li Zhao; Si-Teng Huang; Xin Li; Zhong-Yu Li

record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream performance as latent-action pretraining data is scaled in robotic manipulation, a new setting relative to the language-model scaling claim.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling work in its introduction but does not test loss scaling with language-model parameters, tokens, or compute, or fit those scaling laws. Its own scaling experiment varies the fraction of a robotic video corpus used for pretraining and measures LIBERO-Plus success; these results are recorded under V6.
record.test_reason: Its own Figure 8 experiment pretrains 2B and 4B robot VLA policies on 10–100% of a video corpus and reports LIBERO-Plus success. That is a downstream-versus-data-scale result in a new setting, bearing weakly on V6. No power law is fitted, and the authors say the results do not establish a general scaling law. The system is a vision-language-action policy, not a language model, so the link to V6 rests on reading V6 as a general downstream-scaling claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors report that both models achieve their best LIBERO-Plus success with the full corpus, that 2B improves monotonically while 4B dips from 10% to 30%, and that the results do not establish a general scaling law or isolate data volume from optimization exposure.
record.recipe_differences: Robotic video-pretraining data-fraction sweep with downstream LIBERO-Plus success as the outcome; it does not use the language-model loss-scaling or compute-optimal allocation procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: The data-fraction trend differs by model variant: 2B improves monotonically, whereas 4B dips from 10% to 30% before improving at larger fractions.
record.problems: The scaling results are reported qualitatively in the text and graphically in Figure 8, without numeric data points or stated uncertainty. The authors note that the relationship is not strictly monotonic for every model size and that the study does not isolate pretraining-data volume from all differences in optimization exposure.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant own scaling results were left out. Language-model scaling findings mentioned in citations and background were not entered as rows because they are not this study's results.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute. No loss curves or power-law fits are reported.
Extrapolation from small runs to larger ones.
Architecture shape at a fixed parameter count.
Whether a power-law form holds for robot/video pretraining. Data are scaled, but no functional form is fitted or assessed.

Relation of downstream success to pretraining loss. Scaling in compute. Whether the improvement follows a predictable (fittable) form rather than merely increasing. Only 5 data fractions and 2 model sizes, with no uncertainty reported.
Dependence of fitted exponents or allocations on setup and fitting choices.

missing.what: 2B vs 4B parameter-scale comparisons on downstream benchmarks. 4B beats 2B on LIBERO average (98.8 vs 98.3), LIBERO-Plus (84.7 vs 82.9), RoboTwin (88.6 vs 87.6), VLABench and the real-world tasks. 2B beats 4B on LIBERO-Long (97.8 vs 97.0); the authors note model size 'does not improve every suite'.

Results from the ~1,000-hour pretraining subset versus the full 30.1K-hour corpus. On LIBERO-Plus, 2B scores 82.3 vs 82.9 and 4B scores 84.2 vs 84.7, a small gain for roughly 30x the data. The data mixes differ, so this is not a clean scaling comparison.

record.verdict_notes: Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only in the introduction. The study's scaling result is a small ablation of a robot VLA policy, and its link to the LM-centred V6 is loose; researchers may reasonably treat it as a near-miss. Figure 8 per-point values other than the 100% points cannot be read from the text, and no uncertainty or seeds are reported, so the 4B dip may be within noise.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Architecture-shape effects at fixed parameter count.
Whether a power-law form applies in other modalities or training regimes; the paper scales robotic-video pretraining data but does not fit or assess a power law.
The experiment measures downstream LIBERO-Plus success against pretraining-data fractions, not pretraining loss or scaling in parameter count or compute.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices.

relation.reason: Figure 8 varies pretraining-data fractions for both policy variants and evaluates downstream LIBERO-Plus success.

tranche.reason: The study reports its own downstream-success versus pretraining-data experiment in robotic manipulation, a new setting bearing on V6.

source_check.notes: No scaling function, predictive extrapolation, or uncertainty for Figure 8 is reported. The authors explicitly state that the experiment neither establishes a general scaling law nor isolates data volume from optimization exposure.

statements.correction: 4B: slight LIBERO-Plus success decrease from 10% to 30% pretraining data; improvement at larger fractions; highest success at 100%. Intermediate scores: figure only. Uncertainty: not reported. Offline-metric versus task-success comparison: not measured.
statements.problem: The 4B decrease from 10% to 30% is correctly reported. However, this experiment does not measure an offline metric improving while task success declines. Its mixed data-scaling trajectory warrants limits_scope for the full tested range, rather than an unqualified challenges reading.
